scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that leans toward hard work while granting that talent matters; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: We often wonder whether great artists are born gifted or simply work harder than the rest.
Some believe success in creative fields mainly requires hard work and perseverance, while others believe it mainly requires inborn talent that cannot be learned.
I believe both matter, though I lean toward the view that hard work plays the larger role.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why hard work matters most

sentences.text: First, hard work and perseverance are essential to creative success.
Even gifted people must practise for years to turn raw ability into real skill.
For example, famous writers often rewrite their work many times before it is any good.
This shows that creative achievement depends heavily on patient and stubborn effort.
Talented people who never work hard usually waste the gifts they were born with.
Perseverance also helps artists survive the failure and rejection that creative work brings.
For these reasons, I believe hard work is the larger factor.
Second, however, the opposing view rightly notes that inborn talent also matters.
Some people seem to have a natural gift for music, painting, or storytelling.
Consider a child who plays beautiful music almost effortlessly while others struggle for years.
Such gifts show that talent can give certain people a real head start.
Hard work alone may not reach the heights that genuine talent makes possible.
The greatest creative success often comes when real talent meets relentless effort.
Both qualities, then, play a part in creative achievement.
In conclusion, hard work and perseverance are essential to success in creative fields.
But inborn talent matters too, giving some people a natural advantage.
The finest creative work usually grows where genuine talent and tireless effort meet.
